title: The Great Gouda Quest
markdown:
“Tonight’s the night,” Patch whispered, stuffing shifting as he braced a fuzzy paw on the sill. “The Great Gouda awaits.”

Pearl Decimal preened, smoothing a stray strand of silken mane. “Naturally. As designated strategist, I have calculated the optimal ingress route. Follow me. Try to keep up. And do try not to scuff the dew-kissed primroses. They’re rather sensitive this time of year.”

Leo’s breaths filled the room behind them, already deep. They slipped the window: Patch’s surprisingly strong paw, Pearl’s uncanny lift of a whisper of an inch, enough to clear the frame without a sound. Garden air, cool and thick with damp earth and sleeping roses. Honeysuckle on a passing breeze. The old stone wall loomed; the gap at the bottom, known to brave adventurers and determined garden gnomes, beckoned. Into the ferny woods they tumbled, moss yielding, leaves a thick carpet.

Not a dragon-guarded mountain. The woods behind Leo’s house: familiar, a little wild, perfect for a midnight quest. Faded bunting from summer parties hung between the branches of an ancient oak, dew like tiny forgotten pearls.

“The cheese,” Patch murmured, consulting a crumpled leaf he had designated as a map, “is being presented at the Grand Clearing. For the Moon Moth Festival.”

A chorus of quacks cut the quiet. Tiny ducklings, no bigger than teacups and fluffy as dandelion seeds, waddled into view, bobbing with earnest determination. They were following what they assumed was their mother. Their mother was nowhere to be seen.

“Oh, bother,” Patch sighed. “Not again. Third time this week.”

Pearl huffed, iridescent horn catching moonlight. “Amateurs. They clearly haven’t read the forest’s ceremonial protocol. Auditory reception: substandard. We shall disengage and re-establish our objective. Or perhaps, as the more intellectually gifted of the pair, I should simply carry you. Far more efficient.”

The ducklings had heard the word treat and assumed it was for them. “Quack. Cheese? Quack.” Hopeful little voices.

Patch nudged the smallest with his paw. “Not yet, little ones. A very specific cheese for a very specific occasion. You’ll get your turn.”

They continued. The ducklings trailed like a fluffy quacking entourage. The air grew thicker: damp pine, and then something else — aged, mature, utterly irresistible Gouda, a warm inviting richness.

They paused at the edge of the clearing long enough to look. Ancient toadstools, luminous with phosphorescence, made a natural stage. In the centre, bathed in moonlight, sat a wheel of cheese so grand and golden it looked like a fallen moon. Hedgehogs polished tiny lanterns. A badger in a rather dapper waistcoat waited. A dignified owl perched on a mossy stump. A silent expectant audience.

“Remarkable,” Pearl breathed, superiority briefly forgotten. “The aroma alone is scientifically significant. A complex bouquet of nutty and fruity notes, with a hint of caramelization from the aging process.”

The owl cleared its throat, dry leaves rustling, to begin. Then the ducklings surged forward with a triumphant quack. They had mistaken the magnificent cheese for a giant edible lily pad and were attempting to dive in with gusto.

Patch was a teddy bear, not a knight, but he had a steady paw. He grabbed Pearl’s tail — smooth and cool as polished moonstone — and used her shimmering horn as a lever to vault a low berry bush. He landed with a soft thump beside the cheese, button eyes wide.

“Hold it right there,” he declared, voice wobbling.

Pearl, with a dramatic flourish: “My presence, as a creature of superior intellect and impeccable taste, ensures the preservation of this dairy delicacy. Furthermore, I shall be ensuring its safe and dignified relocation. To a more appropriate venue.”

With a concentrated shimmer of her horn she nudged the cheese, not toward the ducklings, but carefully toward the edge of the clearing. Patch guided it with his paws, worn fur surprisingly adept at steering. The ducklings, bewildered and slightly cross, watched their potential snack roll away. Quacks turned to disappointed murmurs.

“Honestly,” Pearl tutted. “The lack of proper queuing etiquette is simply appalling. One simply must maintain order. A fundamental principle of civilized society, even in the wilderness.”

They nudged the cheese into deeper woods. The ducklings gave up and waddled off in search of a more accessible puddle. Patch and Pearl found a quiet moonlit hollow, dappled with tree-shadow.

Patch caught his breath. “Why the cheese? It was the Moon Moth Festival. I thought it was a special offering for them.”

A small shy field mouse scuttled from beneath the ferns, whiskers twitching. “Oh. That,” it squeaked. “The Moon Moths don’t actually eat cheese. It’s more of a symbolic offering of gratitude for the moonlight. A token. But the cheese maker, old Farmer Giles, made such a magnificent wheel, and he was so proud. He accidentally put it out for collection too early, thinking it was for the village fête. We saw it. We didn’t want him to be sad. We were going to put it back before anyone noticed. We just wanted him to feel appreciated.” The mouse wrung its tiny paws. “We were trying to be kind. To him.”

Patch looked at the cheese, then at Pearl, whose smugness had softened into surprise. “So there was no ceremonial procession. No grand feast for the forest.”

“No,” the mouse said, shoulders slumping. “Just a misunderstanding. And a very, very nice cheese.”

Patch smiled and nudged the Great Gouda with his nose. “A very nice cheese deserves a very nice tasting. Even if it wasn’t for the Moon Moths.”

Pearl, surprising everyone including herself, agreed. “Indeed. A comprehensive sensory analysis is clearly warranted. For scientific posterity, of course. It would be a shame to waste such an opportunity for empirical data collection.”

There, in the quiet hollow, under the watchful moon, teddy Patch, unicorn Pearl Decimal, a shy field mouse, and a few curious hedgehogs who had followed the aroma shared the most unexpectedly acquired wheel of cheese. The scent of aged dairy mingled with cool night air: a touch of melancholy for the intended purpose, and a deeper joy in the shared mistake. No dragon fire. No heroic battles. Only kindness, a wrong cheese in the right hollow, and the rustle of leaves while they ate.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
